context: My grandfather kept his watch in a drawer, wound but never worn. Each night before bed he took it out, turned the small crown exactly twenty times, held it to his ear, and put it back. I asked him once why he bothered winding a watch he never wore. He said it had stopped only once in fifty years, and that once had been enough. He did not explain, and I knew from the way he closed the drawer that I should not ask again. Years later, sorting his papers, I found a telegram dated the spring my grandmother died. It had arrived, my mother told me, while he was at work, and he had not seen it until evening, hours after he might have caught the last train to the hospital. Folded inside it was a repair receipt from a watchmaker, dated the following week.
prompt: Does the passage suggest that a stopped watch played a part in the grandfather missing the chance to reach the hospital in time?
rationale: The watch stopped 'only once', the telegram came the day he missed the last train, and the repair receipt is dated the next week.

context: For centuries, sailors could find their latitude by measuring the height of the Sun or the North Star, but longitude was another matter. Because Earth turns fifteen degrees every hour, a navigator who knew the exact time at home and the local time at sea could work out how far east or west the ship had travelled. The trouble was keeping home time. Pendulum clocks, the most accurate of the day, were useless on a rolling deck, and a clock that drifted just a few seconds a day could put a ship many miles off course after weeks at sea. In the 1700s, the English carpenter and clockmaker John Harrison spent decades building sea clocks that could survive heat, cold and motion. His fourth design, small enough to hold in two hands, kept time well enough on a voyage to the Caribbean to settle the question. Even so, it was years before officials fully accepted that a clock, and not astronomy, had solved the problem.
prompt: Claim: According to the passage, finding longitude at sea depended on knowing the time at a reference place. Judge the claim against the passage.
rationale: The passage says a navigator needed the exact time at home as well as local time.

prompt: Two parents are both heterozygous (Bb) for a trait. Is the probability that a child is homozygous recessive (bb) equal to 1/2?
rationale: The Punnett square gives BB, Bb, Bb, bb, so bb has probability 1/4.

prompt: Is a car that moves at a constant speed around a curve moving with zero acceleration?

prompt: Isn't ice melting into liquid water a physical change rather than a chemical one?

prompt: At a mid-ocean ridge, are the tectonic plates moving toward each other?
